title: The alphabet psalm (Psalm 118 [119])
hook: 176 verses in 22 stanzas, one for each Hebrew letter, all about God's word

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shortest psalm, Laudate Dominum: two verses for the whole world. Your line was all nations. Today, the longest.

Maybe you learned the alphabet with a song. A is for apple, B is for ball, all the way to Z. Children love it because it has an order: you always know where you are and how far is left. Now imagine someone doing that with a prayer. Every letter of their alphabet, in order, eight lines for each. Twenty-two letters. A hundred seventy-six verses. The longest psalm in the Bible, and the longest chapter too.
screen: `A IS FOR APPLE.` → `EIGHT LINES FOR EVERY LETTER.` → `THE LONGEST PSALM OF ALL.`

segments.voice: First, the shape. In Hebrew, this psalm is an acrostic: twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph to tav. All eight lines of the first stanza begin with aleph, every line of the second with beth, and so on to the end. Open a Douay-Rheims and you'll still see the letters printed as little headings: ALEPH, BETH, GHIMEL. English can't keep the trick, but it keeps the signposts. Second, the subject. All hundred seventy-six verses are about one thing: God's word. The poet keeps finding new names for it: law, testimonies, ways, precepts, commandments, justifications, words. Nearly every verse has one. It opens: "Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord." Third, the feeling. You might expect a psalm about law to sound like a rulebook. It sounds like a love letter. Halfway through, the poet says: "O how have I loved thy law, O Lord! it is my meditation all the day." For the psalmist, God's law isn't a fence. It's a gift, the way God has shown himself. Why an alphabet? Nobody knows for certain. Some say it helped people memorize it. Some say it's a way of saying everything, from A to Z, the whole of life, belongs to this love. Jews pray it, and so do Catholics: for centuries monks and priests prayed pieces of it every day in the Divine Office, a stanza or two at a time.
screen: `TWENTY-TWO STANZAS, ALEPH TO TAV.` · `ONE SUBJECT: GOD'S WORD.` · `NOT A RULEBOOK. A LOVE LETTER.` · `EVERYTHING, FROM A TO Z.` · then, large: `O HOW HAVE I LOVED THY LAW, O LORD!`

segments.voice: If you have a Bible nearby, read the first eight verses, the aleph stanza, slowly, out loud or in your head; if not, repeat its opening line: blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Notice which word catches you, and stay with that one.
Aleph. The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, opening the first stanza of the longest psalm: twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter, all about God's word. Today's word.
Your line: a to z of love. From the invitatory, through nephesh, all creation, Vespers and the God who raises the needy, the week ran to the shortest psalm and the longest. A week of psalms, done.

screen: `DAY 182 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A LAMP TO MY FEET.`

howItsDone: Catholics pray portions of Psalm 118 [119] in the Liturgy of the Hours, especially at the midday hours, usually one stanza at a time, and some read one stanza a day as lectio divina.

chat.says: Why is the longest psalm split up by the letters of an alphabet?
options: It's an acrostic: each stanza starts with the next Hebrew letter, all about God's word.
Each letter marks a different author who added a stanza over the centuries.
The letters are a code telling you which day of the month to pray it.
chat.meaning: Twenty-two stanzas, one per Hebrew letter from aleph to tav, all about God's word. Maybe to help memory, maybe to say everything, A to Z.

aleph.meaning: the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet

tav.meaning: the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet

acrostic.meaning: a poem where each part starts with the next letter

notes: Douay-Rheims verses 1 and 97 given from memory; confirm wording.
Letter headings in Douay-Rheims (ALEPH, BETH, GHIMEL): confirm spellings as printed in the Challoner edition.
Names for God's word listed as 'law, testimonies, ways, precepts, commandments, justifications, words': Douay-Rheims uses 'justifications' for statutes; confirm the list against the text.
'Longest chapter in the Bible': commonly stated; confirm.
Week look-back in the carry names days 176–181 (Invitatory, Bless the Lord, All creation, Vespers, From the rising of the sun, The shortest psalm).
Use of Psalm 118 [119] at the little hours of the Divine Office: historically the Roman breviary distributed it across Prime, Terce, Sext and None on Sundays; phrased generally. Confirm.

Audit (second sample): the practice called 'blessed are they who walk in the law of the Lord' 'the line we heard', but the teach quoted the Douay 'Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord'; the practice now repeats the Douay line as taught.
